{{Short description|Type of topological space in mathematics}}
In mathematics, a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> is said to be '''limit point compact'''<ref>The terminology "limit point compact" appears in a topology textbook by [[James Munkres]] where he says that historically such spaces had been called just "compact" and what we now call compact spaces were called "bicompact". There was then a shift in terminology with bicompact spaces being called just "compact" and no generally accepted name for the first concept, some calling it "[[Fréchet]] compactness", others the "Bolzano-Weierstrass property". He says he invented the term "limit point compact" to have something at least descriptive of the property. Munkres, p. 178-179.</ref><ref name="b5SHs">Steen & Seebach, p. 19</ref> or '''weakly countably compact'''<ref name="b5SHs" /> if every infinite subset of <math>X</math> has a [[limit point]] in <math>X.</math> This property  generalizes a property of [[compact spaces]].  In a [[metric space]], limit point compactness, compactness, and [[sequential compactness]] are all equivalent.  For general topological spaces, however, these three notions of compactness are not equivalent.

==Properties and examples==

* In a topological space, subsets without limit point are exactly those that are closed and discrete in the subspace topology.  So a space is limit point compact if and only if all its closed discrete subsets are finite.
* A space <math>X</math> is {{em|not}} limit point compact if and only if it has an infinite closed discrete subspace.  Since any subset of a closed discrete subset of <math>X</math> is itself closed in <math>X</math> and discrete, this is equivalent to require that <math>X</math> has a countably infinite closed discrete subspace.
* Some examples of spaces that are not limit point compact: (1) The set <math>\Reals</math> of all real numbers with its usual topology, since the integers are an infinite set but do not have a limit point in <math>\Reals</math>; (2) an infinite set with the discrete topology; (3) the [[countable complement topology]] on an uncountable set.
* Every [[countably compact space]] (and hence every compact space) is limit point compact.
* For [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]]s, limit point compactness is equivalent to countable compactness.
* An example of limit point compact space that is not countably compact is obtained by "doubling the integers", namely, taking the product <math>X = \Z \times Y</math> where <math>\Z</math> is the set of all integers with the [[discrete topology]] and <math>Y = \{0,1\}</math> has the [[indiscrete topology]].  The space <math>X</math> is homeomorphic to the [[odd-even topology]].<ref>Steen & Seebach, Example 6</ref>  This space is not [[T0 space|T<sub>0</sub>]].  It is limit point compact because every nonempty subset has a limit point.
* An example of T<sub>0</sub> space that is limit point compact and not countably compact is <math>X = \Reals,</math> the set of all real numbers, with the [[Order topology#Left and right order topologies|right order topology]], i.e., the topology generated by all intervals <math>(x, \infty).</math><ref>Steen & Seebach, Example 50</ref>  The space is limit point compact because given any point <math>a \in X,</math> every <math>x<a</math> is a limit point of <math>\{a\}.</math>
* For metrizable spaces, compactness, countable compactness, limit point compactness, and [[Sequentially compact space|sequential compactness]] are all equivalent.
* Closed subspaces of a limit point compact space are limit point compact.
* The continuous image of a limit point compact space need not be limit point compact.  For example, if <math>X = \Z \times Y</math> with <math>\Z</math> discrete and <math>Y</math> indiscrete as in the example above, the map <math>f = \pi_{\Z}</math> given by projection onto the first coordinate is continuous, but <math>f(X) = \Z</math> is not limit point compact.
* A limit point compact space need not be [[pseudocompact]].  An example is given by the same <math>X = \Z \times Y</math> with <math>Y</math> indiscrete two-point space and the map <math>f = \pi_{\Z},</math> whose image is not bounded in <math>\Reals.</math>
* A limit point compact space need not be [[Compact space|compact]]. The [[integers]] with the topology having the basis <math>\mathcal{B} = \{ \{2n, 2n+1\} : n \in \mathbb{Z} \}</math> serve as an example of this fact.<ref>Richmond, p. 125</ref>
* A pseudocompact space need not be limit point compact.  An example is given by an uncountable set with the [[cocountable topology]].
* Every normal pseudocompact space is limit point compact.<ref>Steen & Seebach, p. 20. What they call "normal" is T<sub>4</sub> in wikipedia's terminology, but it's essentially the same proof as here.</ref><br>''Proof'': Suppose <math>X</math> is a normal space that is not limit point compact.  There exists a countably infinite closed discrete subset <math>A = \{x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots\}</math> of <math>X.</math>  By the [[Tietze extension theorem]] the continuous function <math>f</math> on <math>A</math> defined by <math>f(x_n) = n</math> can be extended to an (unbounded) real-valued continuous function on all of <math>X.</math>  So <math>X</math> is not pseudocompact.
* Limit point compact spaces have countable [[Cardinal function#Cardinal functions in topology|extent]].
* If <math>(X, \tau)</math> and <math>(X, \sigma)</math> are topological spaces with <math>\sigma</math> finer than <math>\tau</math> and <math>(X, \sigma)</math> is limit point compact, then so is <math>(X, \tau).</math>
